API/developer services are approved up to Level 3 confidential data. Account access is separate from course, research-use and feature-specific approval.

Codex is included with Harvard ChatGPT Edu licences. ChatGPT Chat and Codex are approved up to Level 3 confidential data; ChatGPT Work requires active monitoring of autonomous sessions for that data level. API keys require separate API Platform access, and connectors require security/privacy approval. Institutional access does not grant assessment permission.

items.oldText: Harvard Medical School responsible AI guidance says users should verify outputs, uphold academic integrity, be transparent about acceptable use, and cite AI contributions appropriately in research and academic work.
items.newText: HMS responsible-use guidance advises users to verify AI outputs, follow applicable faculty/student handbook rules, be transparent about acceptable use and cite AI contributions appropriately. It separately requires attention to confidential data, regulations, sponsor requirements and DUA restrictions; it does not establish assessment permission.

items.oldText: Harvard Medical School lists supported generative AI tools and use cases, including Harvard AI Sandbox, ChatGPT Edu, Adobe Firefly, HMS Azure AI, HUIT API Portal, and Longwood Cluster, with access and training requirements.
items.newText: HMS lists AI Sandbox, Claude, ChatGPT Edu, Microsoft Copilot Premium, Firefly, HMS Azure AI, HUIT API Portal and Longwood Cluster with different eligibility, training, data levels and costs. HMS provides one of Claude, ChatGPT Edu or Copilot Premium per eligible person. HMS Azure AI is a Level 4 service for HMS IT/project developers, and Longwood is a separate Level 4 research environment; this is not blanket Level 4 access for ordinary students.

items.oldText: University-wide: AI meeting assistants (AI note takers or bots) should not be used in Harvard meetings, with the exception of approved tools with contractual protections including enterprise agreements with appropriate security and privacy protections, or tools as part of limited HUIT-directed pilot programs.
items.newText: Harvard meeting guidance says AI assistants should not be used except approved tools with contractual protections or applicable approved pilots/accommodations. Participants must be informed and all must consent before recording/transcription begins. The guidance says not to use assistants when participants object (with a disability-accommodation consultation route), and to disable them in meetings involving Level 3 or higher information. Summaries must be reviewed before limited sharing; retention and litigation holds also apply.

items.oldText: HMS (Harvard Medical School) Academic and Research Integrity guidance: AI tools cannot be listed as authors on a paper. Authors should be transparent when AI tools are used and provide information about how AI tools were used.
items.newText: HMS Academic and Research Integrity guidance says AI tools cannot be listed as authors on papers. Authors should be transparent about using AI tools and explain how the tools were used.

items.oldText: University-wide: Only Harvard-offered versions of generative AI tools carry stated data classification protections. Publicly-available versions of the same tools should not be used for Harvard work. Approved tools (Harvard AI Sandbox, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot Chat, ChatGPT Edu, Adobe Firefly) are approved for Level 3 data and below.
items.newText: HUIT’s general-use comparison applies Level 3-or-below approval and no-vendor-training protection only when logged in with a Harvard account. It does not approve Level 4 data. HMS separately lists special-request Level 4 tools and a Level 2 ceiling for automated meeting assistants. Product access, data approval, DUA/sponsor limits and assessment permission must be checked separately.

Harvard’s Bok Center advises faculty that AI checkers are not currently reliable evidence and may over-identify AI use. Its guidance supports contextual inquiry into student understanding, revision history, timestamps and citations. This does not establish a university-wide ban on all detection or exam-control technologies.

items.oldText: University-wide: Users are responsible for any content they publish or share that includes AI-generated material. AI-generated content may be inaccurate, misleading, entirely fabricated (hallucinations), or contain copyrighted material.
items.newText: Harvard guidance says users are responsible for any content they publish or share that includes AI-generated material, which may be inaccurate, fabricated or copyrighted.

items.oldText: University-wide: Level 2 and above confidential data (including non-public research data, finance, HR, student records, medical information) should not be entered into publicly-available generative AI tools. Such data may only be entered into generative AI tools that have been assessed and approved by Harvard's Information Security and Data Privacy office.
items.newText: Harvard guidance says Level 2 and above confidential data should not be entered into publicly available generative AI tools and must only be entered into tools assessed and approved for that use. HUIT-listed managed general-use tools are approved up to Level 3 with a Harvard account and are not approved for Level 4. Separate HMS Level 4 research/development services require their own access and data-use conditions.

items.oldText: University-wide: Faculty should be clear with students about their policies on permitted uses of generative AI in classes and on academic work. Students are encouraged to ask instructors for clarification about these policies as needed.
items.newText: Harvard guidance recommends that faculty clearly communicate permitted AI uses, if any, in classes and academic work; students are encouraged to ask their instructors for clarification. The applicable School and course rules determine permission.

items.oldText: HGSE (Harvard Graduate School of Education) school-level policy: Unless otherwise specified by the instructor, using generative AI to create all or part of an assignment (e.g., paper, memo, presentation, short response) and submitting it as one's own work violates the HGSE Academic Integrity Policy. Permissible uses include seeking clarification on concepts, brainstorming ideas, or generating scenarios that help contextualize learning.
items.newText: HGSE states that, unless the instructor specifies otherwise, using generative AI to create all or part of a course assignment and submit it as one’s own violates its Academic Integrity Policy. Permissible learning uses include clarification, brainstorming and contextual scenarios; students must discuss uncertain uses with the instructor before use.

items.oldText: HGSE (Harvard Graduate School of Education) school-level policy: For any permitted use of generative AI tools, students must acknowledge and document that use in their assignment submission by explaining what tool(s) were used, prompts provided, and how the output was integrated into the work. Direct citations must use proper citation format.
items.newText: For permitted GenAI use in HGSE assignments, students must acknowledge and document the tools used, prompts if applicable, and how outputs were integrated. Direct citations must use proper citation format.

items.oldText: HGSE (Harvard Graduate School of Education) school-level policy: It is forbidden to make personal recordings of any course meetings, with or without AI tool integrations. Uploading substantial course content is only allowable through the Harvard-approved AI Sandbox.
items.newText: HGSE forbids making personal recordings of course meetings, with or without AI integrations; students needing recordings should discuss them with the instructor. Uploading substantial course content is only allowed through the Harvard-approved AI Sandbox, accessed through individual courses. Assistive-technology AI use must be coordinated with the Office of Student Affairs.

The Harvard Law Graduate Program permits AI queries to clarify exam-relevant concepts while studying, but prohibits queries about exam subject matter during the exam. Pre-writing AI text for incorporation into an exam is not permitted. Instructors may set different rules only when described in writing and communicated to all students. This applies to the Graduate Program policy, not all Harvard courses.

HMS offers one selected managed AI tool per eligible user. Its Sandbox/premium tool rows specify Quad-based faculty, staff and MD/DMD students, with training and some course-based exceptions. Managed tools outside meetings have a Level 3 ceiling; automated meeting assistants have a Level 2 ceiling. HMS Azure AI and Longwood Cluster are separately requested Level 4 environments. DUA, regulatory and sponsor limits still apply even to data-approved tools; no tool is approved for Level 5.

Harvard’s API Platform provides eligible users with self-service AI APIs, pay-as-you-go and limited-access credit-redemption options. Some APIs have narrower eligibility stated in their documentation. Developer services are approved up to Level 3 data. General-use licences do not include API keys; agent/connector features have their own reviewed conditions. Access does not override research data or assessment restrictions.

items.oldText: FAS (Faculty of Arts and Sciences) Office of Undergraduate Education policy: All faculty are required to inform students of the policies governing generative AI use in class. Faculty should post their AI policy on their Canvas site.
items.newText: FAS Office of Undergraduate Education requires faculty to inform students of the policies governing generative AI use in class. It recommends posting the policy on Canvas. This communication requirement does not choose an AI permission policy for the course.

items.oldText: FAS (Faculty of Arts and Sciences) Office of Undergraduate Education guidance: Faculty must get documented permission from students before putting original student content into any generative AI tool. No confidential information can be loaded into generative AI systems since there is no expectation of privacy or confidentiality.
items.newText: FAS OUE guidance requires documented student permission before faculty put original student content into a generative AI tool and says students should be informed of the risks. Its page also contains a broad no-confidentiality statement. HUIT separately describes contractual privacy protections for approved managed services; that data approval does not waive FAS student-content consent or course rules.

Social Studies prohibits generative or agentic AI assistance in submitted coursework, exams/quizzes and all thesis stages by default. Instructors may publish alternative syllabus rules but must require disclosure. Thesis exceptions are case-specific: obtain supervisor approval, submit the AI Policy Attestation request, and secure DUS approval by November 1 of senior year, or April 1 for off-cycle fall seniors. The AI Policy Attestation form is required in consultation with the supervisor at Prospectus submission and again in senior year. Thesis work cannot reuse AI-assisted work from another course merely because that course allowed it. These rules apply to Social Studies requirements.

items.oldText: University-wide: All vendor generative AI tools not currently offered by HUIT must be assessed for risk by Harvard's Information Security and Data Privacy office prior to use in Harvard work. Contact HUIT before procuring any generative AI tool.
items.newText: Harvard guidance requires vendor generative AI tools to be assessed for risk by Harvard Information Security and Data Privacy before use in Harvard work. Users considering tools not currently offered should contact HUIT before procurement. Enabled connectors and new features may need their own review.
